claims.claim: Bryce Lynch praises treasure descriptions that stay terse while being more interesting than a plus-one sword.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of 'The Lions of Tell Arn Part 2', tenfootpole.org, 2026
claims.quote: terse but much more interesting than a Sword, +1
claims.page: Lions of Tell Arn Part 2 review

claims.claim: David Hartlage reports that Gygax's own Castle Greyhawk key usually gave each room a one-line note.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: he usually wrote a 1-line note for each room

claims.claim: David Hartlage says Gygax's generous location descriptions in G1 set the pattern for virtually every adventure that followed.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: Gary’s longer descriptions set the pattern for virtually every adventure to follow.
claims.page: How much description, 'Gary Gygax sets the standard'

claims.claim: David Hartlage argues longer descriptions spare the DM inventing details, whose first ideas tend toward the obvious.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: the ideas that spring to mind first will steer toward the obvious

claims.claim: David Hartlage says an expanded room description pads a good middle sentence like a school paper stretched to length.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: pads it like a school paper stretched to an assigned length

claims.claim: David Hartlage says the custom of long descriptions makes authors write even when they have nothing to add.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: encourages authors to write something even when they have little

claims.claim: David Hartlage says an avalanche of description buries the details that would actually reach play.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: An avalanche of description does more than squander page count.
claims.page: How much description, 'Matching description to a location's purpose'

claims.claim: David Hartlage says a location's description should be as long as the way players will actually engage that location.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: The length of descriptions should match the way players will engage
claims.page: How much description, 'The ideal dungeon description'

claims.claim: David Hartlage tells writers to keep the evocative details out from under lavish description of pallets and rubbish.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: Don’t bury the evocative bits in lavish descriptions
claims.page: How much description, 'The ideal dungeon description'

claims.claim: David Hartlage says descriptions should carry telling details and information he can use in play.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: Descriptions should focus on telling details and plot-critical information
claims.page: How much description, 'The ideal dungeon description'

claims.claim: David Hartlage's test for cutting a description is whether it is the first thing a typical DM would imagine anyway.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: the first thing a typical DM would imagine at the table
claims.page: How much description, 'The ideal dungeon description'

claims.claim: David Hartlage grants that the boxed descriptions in Curse of Strahd are evocative while faulting their use in every empty room.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'How much description should a dungeon key include?', DMDavid, 2016

claims.claim: David Hartlage quotes Bob Bledsaw in Dragon 27 saying judges regarded describing dungeons as their own domain.
claims.source: Bob Bledsaw in Dragon #27, quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: judges felt that the actual description of dungeons was their ‘domain’
claims.page: How much description, 'Tegel Manor and minimal descriptions'

claims.claim: David Hartlage quotes Michael Curtis describing the Stonehell style as the minimum information needed to run the dungeon.
claims.source: Michael Curtis, quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: the minimum amount of information needed to run the dungeon
claims.page: How much description, 'The influence of one-page dungeons'

claims.claim: Luke Gearing's rewrite of his own adventure consisted largely of turning its bullet points back into prose.
claims.source: Luke Gearing, 'Bullet Points vs Prose', lukegearing.blot.im, 2023
claims.quote: A lot of this involves de-bullet pointing the text.
